connection: Session 04 teaches modern relational patterns with a switch expression. This optional sidebar shows the older if/else and switch-statement forms beside the modern switch expression so you can recognize all three in real C# code.
objectives: Recognize the visual and behavioral differences between if/else, a traditional switch statement, and a switch expression.
Explain that switch expressions arrived in C# 8 while traditional switch statements remain valid C#.
Choose a decision form based on the shape of the problem instead of assuming the newest syntax is always required.
Read a small enum as a type with a fixed set of named choices.

visuals.title: if/else asks Boolean questions
visuals.explanation: Each condition is a separate true-or-false question. This form works naturally for ranges, unrelated conditions, and branches that perform several statements.

visuals.title: A traditional switch statement chooses a case
visuals.explanation: The statement form uses case labels, executes statements inside the matching case, and normally uses break to leave that case.

visuals.title: A switch expression produces a value
visuals.explanation: The expression form maps one input to one result. It is concise when the purpose of the decision is to calculate or select a value.

visuals.title: The problem shape guides the syntax
visuals.explanation: All three forms are tools. Prefer the one that communicates the conditions, actions, or returned value most clearly in the codebase you are maintaining.

preQuiz.prompt: Which form was added in C# 8?
preQuiz.explanation: Switch expressions were introduced in C# 8. The older statement forms remain supported.

preQuiz.prompt: Which form naturally handles several unrelated Boolean conditions?
preQuiz.explanation: if/else can ask different Boolean questions in each branch.

preQuiz.prompt: What is an enum in this mini lab?
options: A type with a fixed set of named choices
preQuiz.explanation: CodeStatus restricts the example to the named NotStarted, InProgress, and Completed choices.

concept.title: First, the small enum used by two examples
paragraphs: An enum defines a type with a fixed set of named values. You do not need a full enum lesson here; for now, CodeStatus means that a variable represents one of three named states instead of arbitrary text.
With top-level statements, place the enum declaration after the executable statements in Program.cs.

concept.title: 1. if/else: ask a sequence of questions
paragraphs: Use if/else when branches depend on Boolean conditions, especially ranges or conditions that are not all comparisons against one value.
The Session 04 variance decision is a natural if/else example because it asks whether a decimal is positive, negative, or neither.

concept.title: 2. Traditional switch statement: execute a matching case
paragraphs: The traditional switch statement has existed since early C#. It uses case labels and normally ends each case with break so execution does not continue into another case.
It remains useful in modern C#, particularly when each case performs multiple statements or when you are reading and maintaining an older codebase.

concept.title: 3. Switch expression: map one input to one result
paragraphs: C# 8 introduced the switch expression. Each arm uses => to produce a result, commas separate the arms, and the entire expression is assigned or returned.
Use it when one input is being cleanly translated into one value. It is not a command to replace every if/else or traditional switch statement.

concept.title: A practical decision guide
paragraphs: Choose for clarity in the project and language version you actually maintain. Modern does not automatically mean better for every branch.

rows: You have ranges, unrelated Boolean conditions, or branches with different kinds of work.
One input selects a case, each case performs statements, or an older codebase already uses this form.
One input maps directly to one returned or assigned value.

lab.objective: Run the same CodeStatus mapping through a traditional switch statement and a modern switch expression, then choose the clearer form for three scenarios.
lab.startingCondition: This is an optional isolated exercise after Session 04. It does not change the TimeClock solution or block Session 05.

steps.text: Create and enter a temporary console project outside the TimeClock repository.

dotnet new console -n DecisionSyntaxSideLab
cd DecisionSyntaxSideLab

Run the project. Expect Traditional: Coding is in progress. Then identify switch, case, break, and default in the code before continuing.
Above Console.WriteLine, add the modern switch expression. Keep the traditional statement so both forms can be compared in one file.
Directly below the traditional Console.WriteLine, add this second output statement.
Run again. Both output lines should end with Coding is in progress.

steps: Change codeStatus to CodeStatus.NotStarted and then CodeStatus.Completed, running after each edit. Confirm both decision forms produce the same meaning for every enum value.

Choose a form for each scenario and explain why: a decimal temperature range; an enum case that logs two messages and updates a counter; an enum translated directly into display text. Suggested choices are if/else, traditional switch statement, and switch expression respectively, but your explanation matters more than memorizing that order.
lab.expectedBehavior: The traditional switch statement and modern switch expression produce equivalent messages for all three CodeStatus values, while their syntax and best-fit use cases remain visibly different.

expectedFiles.why: Compare syntax without changing the cumulative TimeClock project.

commit: Not applicable — optional side lab; no TimeClock repository changes.
review: The enum is declared once and contains exactly three named choices.
Every traditional switch case assigns a message and exits with break.
Every switch-expression arm produces a string and ends with a comma except the completed expression's semicolon.
The comparison explains when each form communicates intent clearly rather than declaring one universal winner.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does the traditional switch example use break?
options: To leave the matching case after its statements run
postQuiz.explanation: break transfers control out of the switch statement after the selected case finishes.

postQuiz.prompt: Which form best fits mapping one CodeStatus value directly to one string in C# 8 or later?
postQuiz.explanation: A switch expression concisely represents one-input-to-one-result mapping.

postQuiz.prompt: Does the existence of switch expressions make traditional switch statements invalid?
options: No; they remain valid and can be clearer for statement-heavy cases
Only enums can use the older form
postQuiz.explanation: New syntax adds another option; it does not remove the traditional statement.

reflections: Which visual clues immediately distinguish a switch statement from a switch expression?
Why might a team keep a traditional switch statement even after upgrading to C# 8 or later?
When does compact syntax improve clarity, and when might it hide too much from a beginner?
whatBreaks: Skipping this optional side lab does not break the TimeClock path. You would only lose practice recognizing older switch statements and comparing the three decision forms deliberately.
summary: if/else asks flexible Boolean questions. A traditional switch statement selects and executes a case using case, break, and default. A C# 8+ switch expression maps one input directly to one result using => arms and an optional _ fallback. All three remain useful when their shape matches the problem.
